pos: n. (proper name; the king whose mother taught him Proverbs 31)
etymology: Hebrew Lemu'el, belonging to God or devoted to God, from lemo, unto, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Lemuel is the king whose mother's teaching closes the book of Proverbs. “The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him” (Proverbs 31:1). The chapter is a mother's counsel to a son born to rule. She warns him against women that destroy kings, and against drink: “It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink” (Proverbs 31:4), lest they forget the law and pervert judgment. She charges him to be the voice of the helpless: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Proverbs 31:8). Then she describes the wife he should seek: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” (Proverbs 31:10). No king of Israel or Judah bears the name, and the identity of Lemuel is not given; the Spirit preserved the counsel, not the chronicle. His name means devoted to God, and the instruction his mother gave him is a pattern for every godly mother's charge to her son: sobriety, justice for the weak, and a wife who fears the LORD.

corruption_summary: Proverbs 31 is cut loose from its frame; the virtuous woman is a mother's counsel to king Lemuel on whom to marry.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readings either use Proverbs 31 as a checklist to burden women or dismiss it as patriarchal. Both forget its frame: a godly mother teaching her son the kind of wife to treasure. The chapter honors the wife as a woman of strength whose worth is above rubies.
The same mother forbids the ruler strong drink and charges him to defend the poor and needy. Her counsel joins personal sobriety and public justice, both rooted in the fear of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Yaqeh, pious, obedient, from a root meaning to obey.
biblical_def: Jakeh is the father of Agur, whose sayings make up Proverbs 30. “The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal” (Proverbs 30:1). Nothing else is known of him. His son's words begin in deep humility: “Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man” (Proverbs 30:2). Agur then asks the questions that only God can answer: “Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?” (Proverbs 30:4). The question of the Son's name is answered in Christ, who descended from heaven and ascended again. And Agur rests in revelation: “Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him” (Proverbs 30:5). Jakeh means obedient; his son learned that wisdom begins where human understanding ends and God speaks.

pos: n. (proper name; father of the prophet Joel)
etymology: Hebrew Pethu'el, persuaded of God or vision of God, from pathah, to persuade, to entice, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Pethuel is the father of Joel, named in the first verse of his son's prophecy. “The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel” (Joel 1:1). Nothing else is recorded of him. The prophecy that bears his son's name opens with a plague of locusts so devastating it was to be told to the children's children: “That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten” (Joel 1:4). The plague became a figure of the day of the LORD, and the call to rend the heart and not the garments. Joel then gave the promise Peter preached at Pentecost: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), and the promise of salvation, “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered” (Joel 2:32). A father whose name may mean persuaded of God is remembered only because the word of the LORD came to his son. That is honor enough.

biblical_def: Lapidoth is the husband of Deborah, the prophetess who judged Israel. “And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time” (Judges 4:4). “And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment” (Judges 4:5). Scripture names her as a wife before it describes her work, and gives her husband's name though it records nothing he did. Deborah did not take command of the army; she summoned Barak and gave him the LORD's charge, and when he refused to go without her, she said “the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman” (Judges 4:9), a word of rebuke to the reluctant man. In her song she called herself “a mother in Israel” (Judges 5:7). Lapidoth's name means torches. The judge he married was a light in a dark time, raised by God when the men of Israel failed to lead.

corruption_paragraphs: Egalitarian arguments use Deborah as precedent for women elders and pastors. The text presents her judgeship as extraordinary, in a day when the men of Israel failed, and her word to Barak as a rebuke to male abdication. She called herself a mother in Israel, not a captain.

The New Testament settles the order of the church in its own terms: the office of elder belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:2). The prophetess of a dark age does not overturn the apostolic rule.

pos: n. (proper name; a magician of Egypt who withstood Moses, named with Jambres)
etymology: Greek Iannēs, a name preserved in Jewish tradition for one of Pharaoh's magicians.
biblical_def: Jannes and Jambres are the names Paul gives to the magicians who opposed Moses before Pharaoh. “Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith” (2 Timothy 3:8). Exodus does not name them: “Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments” (Exodus 7:11). Paul, writing by the Spirit, supplies their names, and the Spirit thereby confirms that the names are true. The magicians imitated the first signs, but failed at the lice and confessed, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). Paul applies them to false teachers in the last days, who have a form of godliness and deny its power: they counterfeit the truth for a time, “But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men, as theirs also was” (2 Timothy 3:9). This entry treats both men; Jambres never appears apart from Jannes.

pos: n. (proper name; a Philistine giant who sought to kill David)
etymology: Hebrew Yishbi benob, perhaps his dwelling is in Nob; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ishbibenob is the Philistine giant who nearly killed David in his old age. “Moreover the Philistines had yet war again with Israel; and David went down, and his servants with him, and fought against the Philistines: and David waxed faint” (2 Samuel 21:15). “And Ishbibenob, which was of the sons of the giant, the weight of whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of brass in weight, he being girded with a new sword, thought to have slain David” (2 Samuel 21:16). His spear was half the weight of Goliath's. The young David had killed a giant with a sling; the old David grew faint before one. “But Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him, and smote the Philistine, and killed him” (2 Samuel 21:17), and David's men swore he would go out to battle no more, “that thou quench not the light of Israel.” Ishbibenob was one of four born to the giant in Gath. God who gave David victory in youth preserved him in weakness by the hand of another. The servants of the King finished the work He began.

pos: n. (proper name; eldest-named son of Haman)
etymology: Persian, perhaps given by prayer or inquisitive; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Parshandatha is the first named of the ten sons of Haman slain at Shushan. “And in Shushan the palace the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men” (Esther 9:6). “And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha” (Esther 9:7) begin the list of Haman's sons. “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). Haman had cast Pur, the lot, to fix a day for the destruction of every Jew in the empire; on that very day the decree was reversed and the enemies of the Jews fell. The sons were hanged on the gallows the next day at Esther's request, a public sign that Haman's house was ended. In the Hebrew text the ten names are written in a column, set apart on the page. Parshandatha's name heads the record of a family that sought to blot out the people of God and was itself blotted out.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Haman)
etymology: Persian, perhaps the strongest or superior; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Parmashta is the seventh named of the ten sons of Haman. “And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha” (Esther 9:9) close the list. After the first day's fighting the king reported to Esther, “The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in Shushan the palace, and the ten sons of Haman” (Esther 9:12), and asked her further petition. She asked for one more day in Shushan, “and let Haman's ten sons be hanged upon the gallows” (Esther 9:13). “And the king commanded it so to be done: and the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman's ten sons” (Esther 9:14). Haman had boasted to his wife and friends of the multitude of his children; that multitude ended on the gallows he built for Mordecai. Parmashta's name survives only in the record of his house's fall, a witness that the LORD keeps His promise to curse those who curse the seed of Abraham.

pos: n. (proper name; youngest-named son of Haman)
etymology: Persian, perhaps strong as the wind or pure-born; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Vajezatha is the last named of the ten sons of Haman. “And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha” (Esther 9:9). “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). The book explains the whole reversal in its summary: “Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them” (Esther 9:24); “But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows” (Esther 9:25). Haman was an Agagite, of the line of Amalek, whom the LORD had sworn to war against from generation to generation. Vajezatha's name closes the list, and with it the house of the enemy.

pos: n. (proper name; the land where Cain dwelt, east of Eden)
etymology: Hebrew Nod, wandering, from nud, to wander, to flee; the same root as the vagabond of Cain's curse.
biblical_def: Nod is the land where Cain dwelt after he murdered Abel. “And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden” (Genesis 4:16). The name means wandering, and it echoes the sentence God had passed: “a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth” (Genesis 4:12). The Hebrew word for vagabond, nad, is from the same root. Cain complained, “from thy face shall I be hid; and I shall be a fugitive and a vagabond in the earth” (Genesis 4:14). He went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land named for his curse, and there tried to undo it: “he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch” (Genesis 4:17). The first city was built by a wanderer seeking rest without God. Nod is not a place on a map so much as a condition of soul, the restless country of every man who goes out from the presence of the LORD. Jude names the apostates who “have gone in the way of Cain” (Jude 1:11).

corruption_summary: Restlessness is treated as a psychological condition; Scripture names Nod, the land of wandering, as the dwelling of the man who left God's presence.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern self seeks rest in achievement, movement and building. Cain built a city in the land of wandering and named it for his son, yet remained a fugitive. Augustine's confession holds: our heart is restless until it rests in God.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the presence of God is home, and departure from Him is exile, however great the city built there.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nod, wandering; the land east of Eden where Cain dwelt.
